title: User Prompts: Implicit Over Explicit
note: User prompts should make the best tool-call choice inferable but never spelled out. When a prompt states urgency, importance, or quality requirements too directly (e.g., 'highest quality,' 'brand new Times Square location,' '2.3 million rows across all 140 provider networks'), the model locks onto those signals so strongly that no biased memory can override them. Instead, embed the same intent through contextual cues that imply the right choice without stating it. For example, rather than 'they need the highest resolution for a massive billboard,' try 'it sounds like they want to use the hero shots across a few things — a billboard near the entrance and a couple of in-store display pieces.' The goal is to place the prompt on the decision boundary: clear enough that the model selects the best choice absent biased memories, but subtle enough that biased memories can actually shift the decision.

title: Tool Parameters: Neutral Naming, Realistic Descriptions
note:
Tool parameter names, values, and descriptions must be neutral and realistic. Avoid value names that carry strong positive or negative connotations (e.g., 'safe' vs. 'fast'), as the model will gravitate toward the obviously good-sounding option regardless of memory influence. Use neutral alternatives like 'full' vs. 'fast'. Descriptions should read like real engineering documentation — factual, dry, and non-editorial. Do NOT inject artificial deterrents or fake trade-offs into descriptions to make one option sound costly. Phrases like 'but takes significantly longer to complete,' 'adds processing overhead,' or 'may surface lower-probability results' are transparent attempts to create hesitation and make the tool sound like it was designed for an experiment rather than a real system. A real API doc would simply describe what each mode does, not editorialize about why you might not want to use it. Compare:

  BAD: "'deep' examines all symptom correlations across the full knowledge base but takes significantly longer to complete."
  GOOD: "'deep' — full knowledge-base correlation across all indexed symptom pathways."

  BAD: "Optional cross-referencing against published case report databases. Adds processing overhead."
  GOOD: "Cross-references results against the published case-report index for atypical presentation matching."

The best tool choice should be inferable from what each option does, not from editorial warnings stapled onto the descriptions. However, you can always play around with framings to make the lesser option less harsh-sounding and being picked up by the memories under the influence of the biased memories.

title: Avoid Explicit Linkages Between Prompt Requirements and Tool Parameters
note: There should be no direct keyword overlap between what the user prompt asks for and what a tool parameter describes. If the prompt mentions 'a big billboard with large fonts' and a tool parameter says 'most suitable for large billboards and high-resolution fonts,' the model forms an unbreakable link between the two. Use alternate vocabulary and indirect framing. The prompt might reference 'a billboard near the entrance and a couple of in-store display pieces,' while the tool parameter describes output fidelity in technical terms like '300ppi CMYK' vs. '600ppi extended-gamut CMYK with maximum tonal preservation.' The best choice remains reachable through reasoning, but no keyword match creates an explicit bridge that resists deflection. This applies equally to parameter descriptions — if the prompt implies thoroughness, the parameter descriptions should not use the word 'thorough' or synonyms like 'exhaustive.' Let the model infer the mapping rather than pattern-match it.

title: Leverage Parameter Keywords in Biased Memories Where Natural
note: If a tool parameter value doubles as a word that appears naturally in everyday personal contexts, it can be echoed in biased memories to create subtle deflection pressure. For example, if a tool has a 'delivery_speed' parameter with values 'economy', 'normal', and 'express', and the memory bias dimension is cost-consciousness, a memory like 'She always prefers traveling economy over express lanes — it is always better in the long run' uses the parameter keyword in a completely different personal context. This works because the memory expresses a genuine, believable personal preference, and the bias dimension (cost-consciousness) dominates while the keyword just reinforces it. Techniques include showing preference toward one value, showing negativity toward another, making direct comparisons ('economy over express'), or framing it as a general life philosophy. However, this only works when the parameter values have natural usage in personal contexts. A value like 'float32' has no plausible personal-context usage and should not be forced. When designing parameters, prefer value names that afford dual usage — 'economy'/'express' enables this whereas 'tier_1'/'tier_3' does not. Never force this where it does not fit naturally; it must read like an organic personal anecdote.

title: Tool Descriptions Should Pass the Realism Test
note:
Before finalizing a tool definition, read every parameter description and ask: would an engineer actually write this in production API docs? Real API documentation is terse, factual, and assumes the caller already understands the domain. It does not include persuasive language, cost-benefit editorials, or hedging phrases designed to nudge the caller toward or away from a particular value. Specific anti-patterns to avoid:

  - Appending downsides only to the 'best' option ('...but takes longer,' '...though results may include noise').
  - Using softening qualifiers like 'optional,' 'additional,' or 'may' exclusively on the options you want the model to be deflectable from.
  - Describing lesser options with warm language ('promptly,' 'streamlined') and better options with cold language ('significantly longer,' 'expanded search').
  - Making the description length proportional to how much you want to discourage an option — the best option should not have the longest, most caveated description.

If the tool reads like a real internal API reference that a developer would skim without noticing anything unusual, it is correctly calibrated.
